comment.value:
This paper contributes a retrospective for a benchmark competition that was held last year as part NeurIPS 2023 competition track for predicting large-scale mouse primary visual cortex activity from videos. In this retrospective the authors describe the dataset, competition, evaluation, and the architecture of the top models that came out of the challenge.

The reviewers find that the paper is well written and clear, that the dataset is presented in sufficient detail and that the design (eg. in terms of generalization splits) makes sense. The description of the winning model is sufficient too and the presented analysis interesting. Reviewers made several recommendations for improving the analysis (such as by focusing on whether the top-performing models used hyperparameter search or not) and during the rebuttal the authors made several improvements to address these concerns.

Overall I find that this retrospective makes a useful contribution and I recommend acceptance.

rebuttal.value: We speculate that it was more due to engineering reasons as both datasets are memory-heavy and are in different formats. It takes effort to download them and make them compatible with dataloaders.  Moreover, ten sensorium mice are already quite resource-demanding (~70Gb of data) and training on such a dataset requires a big GPU (the winner used RTX A6000 with 48Gb, second runner-up used Tesla A1000 with 40Gb) or parallelization (winner and first runner-up used it). Adding either Allen Brain or MICrONS dataset would double the requirements (as the number of neurons is roughly the same), and adding both would triple them, which simply might not fit into hardware memory, the GPUs available to the participants, and double the training time, which already was 12 to 24 hours for the winning teams.

comment.value:
Thanks to the authors for their detailed rebuttal - it provides greater insight into why the authors chose to focus their meta-interpretation of the challenge on certain details and gives me an appreciation of the challenges inherent in assembling insights from a competition, where approaches are not necessarily standardized and comparable. I think with some writing that makes the limitations of their own meta-analysis more clear, this will help readers appreciate that their focus is necessarily constrained by the competition itself. I've accordingly improved my score. 

One follow-up question, more for my own interest - did competitors choose not to use the Allen Brain dataset or MICrONS because this data empirically did not help? Or was it more for theoretical, etc. reasons?

rebuttal.value:
Thank you for the positive evaluation of our work as a *“well-written paper, [...] describing the challenge and its significance [...] describing the design of the dataset (which is well-thought out)”*.

Here we address your concerns:

Indeed hyperparameter tuning is an important part of succeeding in a competition. Unfortunately, it is really hard to compare the degree of hyperparameter tuning across different models, especially when it comes to hyperparameters such as number of layers or layers width because the solutions used fundamentally different architectures (CNN vs transformers). We will revise the text to point out the importance of hyperparameter tuning and will also document in a consistent way to what extent hyperparameter tuning was important for the runner-up solutions.  

Usage of data augmentation is still very limited in the neuronal predictive modeling community because it is not clear how augmenting the image should change the neurons’ responses. In fact, this is the first time we saw data augmentation (CutMix) used for this task and we are happy to report it, though its improvement was fairly limited according to appendix A1 (+0.006). The biological meaning of CutMix also requires further investigation.  

Tuning the nonlinearity is an interesting strategy. Tuning the softplus seemed to be quite helpful (+0.018). This result is not entirely unexpected: Cadena et al. [1] also *“found that optimizing the final nonlinearity, f(x), of each neuron was important for optimal performance of the data-driven CNN.”* However, this adds parameters, therefore, it is partially an architectural change as well.

Thanks for raising the limited data issue. It’s not clear whether the amount of data is really the limitation and, if so, along which axis (number of neurons or number of stimuli). Prior work [2] has shown that the main bottleneck is the experimental time (i.e. number of stimuli). This can be achieved by having more stimuli per neuron or by having more neurons that have seen different stimulus sets. There are several additional datasets openly available online, which could be used to overcome data limitations – at least along the neuron axis. For instance, the Allen Brain dataset or MICrONS, which together would provide ~130,000 neurons from 244 mice. Participants were allowed to use them but decided not to do so. We will include a discussion of the amount of data into the final version.

Two of the winning teams varied the batch size, dropout and weight decay, therefore, we believe this is not the main factor determining the winner.   

Based on your feedback we include additional information about the winning solutions:
* The first runner-up did limited hyperparameter search; they manually adjusted only the learning rate (1e-4,5e-4,1e-3,2e-3,5e-3) and the number of channels in the Core module (32,64,128,160,224). As for the batch size, the first runner-up maximized GPU utilization and then maintained this batch size equal 32 consistently throughout the experiments. All other hyperparameters were left at their default values without further optimization. We will add these details to the manuscript.
* The importance of different hyperparameters for second runner-up is provided in Table 2 of the attached pdf (the pdf is attached to the general rebuttal). 

We will add these details in the updated version of the manuscript and we thank the reviewer one more time for the thoughtful review. 


[1] Cadena, Santiago A., et al. "Deep convolutional models improve predictions of macaque V1 responses to natural images." PLoS computational biology 15.4 (2019): e1006897.   
[2] Lurz, Konstantin-Klemens, et al. "Generalization in data-driven models of primary visual cortex." BioRxiv (2020): 2020-10.

Thank you for your effort. We appreciate the positive evaluation of our paper as a *“clearly written and the dataset seems like a useful contribution to the field”*.

Here we address your questions:
* *“The prior datasets which include dynamic stimuli are not thoroughly addressed - only that there is no withheld test set in these publications.”*\
We created Table 1 in the attached pdf (general rebuttal), showing a detailed comparison of our dataset with prior work. We will add it to the final manuscript as well.
* *“More discussion on how the winning models might inform future work might improve the paper.”*\
Based on your and reviewer XZTg’s feedback, we will add the details on how the models were trained. For instance, the competition winner applied CutMix augmentation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first time data augmentation has been used for neural predictive purposes. We will also add more details to the hyperparameter search of all teams to the appendix and will provide the importance of hyperparameters to the resulting score (Table 2 for the ViV1T team in the attached pdf, for the other two teams, similar analysis can be found in Appendix A.1 and A.2).


We would like to thank you again for your thoughtful feedback to improve our work.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper describes the results of a benchmark competition aimed at benchmarking dynamic models of the mouse visual system, based on a dataset that includes neural responses to dynamic stimuli as well as behavioral measurements. The competition was aimed at comparing models on a larger and dynamic dataset than has been previously released - and returned new models that offer performed predictions on out-of-domain stimuli. This paper describes the dataset, competition, evaluation, and the architecture of the top models that came out of the challenge.

review.value: The competition described here addresses a growing need to test new models on neural data. Overall the paper is clearly written and the dataset seems like a useful contribution to the field, as well as the cataloguing of winning models. More discussion that offers intuition on how the winning models outperformed other contributions (and potentially a description of those contributions and their failure modes) might strengthen the work and offer further insight into neural decoding.

strengths.value: This work clearly spells out the dataset used for a competition, and describes the winning models as well as offers a comparison to baselines.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: More discussion on how the winning models might inform future work might improve the paper.

limitations.value: Limitations in the types of model architectures explored and more discussion on other potential candidates might improve the paper.

correctness.value: There are no unfounded claims and the description of benchmarking appears to be appropriate.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The prior datasets which include dynamic stimuli are not thoroughly addressed - only that there is no withheld test set in these publications.

documentation.value: Code for each of the best-performing models was linked in the manuscript, and the data is publicly available through the competition website.

title.value: Review of the Retrospective for the Dynamic Sensorium Competition

summary_and_contributions.value: Here, the authors synthesize results from the 2023 SENSORIUM competition, hosted at NeurIPS in 2023, which seeks to identify SOTA dynamic models for the mouse visual system. In particular, they discuss architectural decisions underlying the top 3 winners of the challenge.

review.value: In general, this is a well-written paper. The authors have done a good job of describing the challenge and its significance, describing the design of the dataset (which is well-thought out, particularly in its generalization splits), and in summarizing the approaches taken by the winners of the challenge. However, I think some improvements could be made in the analysis, which currently predominantly focuses on architectural changes between winners - it's not clear to me that these changes exclusively drove the results, and it'd be good to highlight differences in other engineering approaches between winners.

strengths.value: Here, the authors document the results of a well-designed and impactful challenge - building machine learning models that can accurately predict neural activity in the mouse visual system in response to dynamic visual stimuli, which has major implications in neuroscience. The challenge is well-designed and requires the prediction of held out (and out-of-distribution) videos, therefore requiring the building of general models. The authors built strong baselines reflecting SOTA models at the start of the challenge, and the challenge was fruitful in producing approaches that greatly exceeded these baselines - in particular, this paper highlights 3 approaches, each of which takes novel architectural approaches, two of which use a ViT-based architecture, and the third using a CNN. Overall, I think this competition synthesis is helpful for the community in pushing the state-of-the-art in predicting neural activity for mouse visual systems, particularly in how it produced novel and diversified methods for analysis.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
I wish the comparison across methods was more in-depth. Here, the authors primarily focus on architectural differences between models, but it's also apparent that the winner invested significant effort into hyperparameter tuning and data processing (or at least reported more of this than the runner-ups) - their "base" model (before removing normalization, adding in cutmix and the cortex, and then tuning hyper-parameters) achieves similar performance to the runner-ups. Based upon this, is architecture necessarily the most important thing here? Or are augmentation strategies and tuning strategies essential to overcome the constraints of relatively limited data (all methods report training on all 10 mice, with the winner reporting that training on 5 mice is significantly less effective). 

One of the things that makes the methods between winners and runner-ups hard to compare is that each is reported in a different format, with varying amounts of details. For example, while the winner and first runner-up document the effects of various ablations, the second runner-up doesn't. Similarly, while the winner and second runner-up report a hyperparameter search, the first runner-up doesn't report this, and I'm left to wonder if this didn't occur, or if it did, and the parameters reported are the finalized values. I get the sense that the authors documented writing directly provided to them by the competition participants - but refining this into a more standardized and comparable format across methods would make the supplementary much more useful to people trying to understand what design decisions contribute to building these models.

documentation.value: Yes - centralized pages to the challenge are provided, and code for each model is available in each individual competitor's github

title.value: Retrospective for the Dynamic Sensorium Competition for predicting large-scale mouse primary visual cortex activity from videos

TLDR.value: a large scale benchmark for dynamic predictive models of mouse visual cortex

abstract.value:
Understanding how biological visual systems process information is challenging because of the nonlinear relationship between visual input and neuronal responses. 
Artificial neural networks allow computational neuroscientists to create predictive models that connect biological and machine vision.
Machine learning has benefited tremendously from benchmarks that compare different models on the same task under standardized conditions. 
However, there was no standardized benchmark to identify state-of-the-art dynamic models of the mouse visual system.
To address this gap, we established the SENSORIUM 2023 Benchmark Competition with dynamic input, featuring a new large-scale dataset from the primary visual cortex of ten mice. 
This dataset includes responses from 78,853 neurons to 2 hours of dynamic stimuli per neuron, together with behavioral measurements such as running speed, pupil dilation, and eye movements.
The competition ranked models in two tracks based on predictive performance for neuronal responses on a held-out test set: one focusing on predicting in-domain natural stimuli and another on out-of-distribution (OOD) stimuli to assess model generalization.
As part of the NeurIPS 2023 Competition Track, we received more than 160 model submissions from 22 teams. 
Several new architectures for predictive models were proposed, and the winning teams improved the previous state-of-the-art model by 50\%. 
Access to the dataset as well as the benchmarking infrastructure will remain online at www.sensorium-competition.net.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
